title: Clomiphene citrate for men with hypogonadism: a systematic review and meta-analysis
article_subtype: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials and observational cohort studies
condition_or_topic: Clomiphene citrate therapy for men with hypogonadism
clinical_background: Male hypogonadism involves symptomatic testosterone insufficiency that can affect sexual function, mood, muscle strength, and quality of life. Symptomatic hypogonadism affects between 2.1% and 5.7% of men aged 40–79 years, with prevalence rising with age and certain comorbidities. Testosterone therapy (TTh) is the first-choice treatment, but its suppression of endogenous testosterone can impair fertility; other reported adverse effects include increases in prostate volume, prostate specific antigen (PSA), hematocrit (Ht), and serum estrogen. Clomiphene citrate (CC) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator that promotes gonadotropin release and testicular testosterone production. It is used off-label in men, particularly when preserving fertility matters, but its effectiveness for hypogonadism has been uncertain.
objectives: Assess the effectiveness and safety of CC therapy in men with hypogonadism through a systematic review and meta-analysis.
Evaluate serum hormone concentrations before and during CC treatment as the primary outcome.
Evaluate hypogonadal symptoms, metabolic and lipid profiles, side effects, and safety measures as secondary outcomes.
clinical_question: In men aged ≥ 18 years with hypogonadism (Patient), how does CC treatment (Intervention), compared with measurements before treatment and with comparator groups where available (Comparator), affect serum hormone concentrations, hypogonadal symptoms, metabolic and lipid profiles, side effects, and safety measures (Outcome)?
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of intervention and observational studies, conducted in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) and registered as CRD42021246588. EMBASE, PubMed, and Cochrane were searched in May 2021; reference lists were also searched. Two reviewers independently selected studies. The review included four randomized controlled trials and 15 observational cohort studies, of which 11 were retrospective and four prospective.

population.description: Men with hypogonadism treated with clomiphene citrate. Across the included studies, 1642 patients received CC; 1279 patients treated with CC were represented in the meta-analysis.
inclusion_criteria: Intervention or observational studies written in English or Dutch that assessed the effectiveness of CC in men with hypogonadism aged ≥ 18 years.
Studies reporting at least a hormonal assessment during CC treatment; assessment of hypogonadal symptoms was preferred.
exclusion_criteria: Treatment with enclomiphene, zuclomiphene, or CC combined with another medicine as the intervention under evaluation.

Populations selected for specific chronic disorders, including HIV, cancer, osteoporosis, severe kidney/liver disease, depression, hemochromatosis, acromegaly, polycythemia, Alzheimer, eating disorder, sickle cell disease, and retardation.
Populations selected for genetic disorders, including Klinefelter, Prader–Willi, Kallman, and Bardet–Biedl.
Case series n < 5, letters to the editor, pilot studies, reviews, comments, and animal studies.
population.mean_age: Study mean ages for patients treated with CC were between 29 and 62 years.

interventions: Clomiphene citrate (CC); reported dosing varied between 25 and 50 mg per day or 25, 50, or 100 mg every other day.

primary: Serum hormone concentrations before and during treatment

statistical_methods: Results were summarized as counts, percentages, or means with standard deviations (SD). Outcomes reported by three or more studies were pooled when means and SD were available, using Review Manager (RevMan) 5.4. Standard errors were converted to SD, and medians with interquartile ranges were converted to means with SD. Inverse-variance weighting was used to pool before-versus-during-treatment effects as mean differences or standardized mean differences with confidence intervals (CI); standardized mean differences were used when outcome units differed. Heterogeneity was assessed by examining forest plots and using the χ2 test and I2 statistic. Sensitivity analyses were restricted separately to randomized controlled trials and to studies rated as strong quality. For two studies reporting age subgroups, the subgroup with the largest sample was selected for meta-analysis.
follow_up: CC treatment and follow-up durations ranged from 1.5 to 52 months.
quality_assessment_tool: Effective Public Health Practice Project Quality Assessment Tool (EPHPP)
interpretation: The authors interpret the rise in TT, FT, LH, FSH, and estradiol during CC treatment as evidence that it stimulates endogenous testosterone production in men with hypogonadism. TT response rates ranged between 62% and 81%, and ADAM scores improved. They caution that clinical symptom improvement is less certain because placebo-controlled studies also found symptom improvement. Evidence remains insufficient to establish effects on metabolic and lipid measures. Reported adverse effects were generally uncommon, but longer-term safety and the persistence of benefit after stopping CC remain uncertain.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Taylor and Levine (2010) (n = 103) found no difference in serum TT outcomes between CC and testosterone gel. Ramasamy et al. (2014) (n = 124) likewise found comparable TT outcomes with those treatments, but a greater TT increase with testosterone injections; that study found no ADAM outcome difference between CC and TTh. Guay et al. (2003) suggested that TT might remain elevated after CC withdrawal without testing that proposal. In contrast, Patel et al. (2015) (n = 27) found TT below <300 ng/dL in 78% of patients after 3 months off treatment and in all patients after 6 months. Other cited studies reported differing results after withdrawal. Placebo-controlled trials also complicate interpretation of symptom improvement: one (n = 17) found that participants could not distinguish CC from placebo by their symptoms, while another found similar overall improvement in both groups. An earlier study of 200 patients reported less polycythemia with CC than with TTh.
clinical_implications: CC may address biochemical testosterone insufficiency while preserving fertility; the authors also describe it as less expensive and noninvasive than TTh.
The authors consider continued CC treatment probably necessary to maintain its biochemical and clinical effects, although findings after withdrawal differ across studies.
Symptom response cannot be inferred reliably from the overall ADAM result alone: hypogonadal symptoms have multiple contributing causes, and placebo groups also improved in included trials.
The included studies reported few adverse effects, but the authors identify elevated hematocrit and a possible paradoxical decline in testicular function as concerns requiring attention.
practice_implications: The authors recommend considering CC for men with symptomatic hypogonadism, particularly those with a current or future wish to have children.
In the authors’ opinion, a treatment approach is to begin CC at 25 mg every other day and adjust the dose according to achieved serum TT or symptom improvement.
The authors advocate developing and implementing a new or updated questionnaire to assess symptoms of hypogonadism.
limitations: Studies missed by the search could have influenced the meta-analysis, despite the extensive search and examination of reference lists.

Most analyses had substantial heterogeneity in a limited evidence base. The authors cite differences in study design, CC dosage, hormone measurement, and the clarity or strictness of eligibility criteria.
Methodological quality varied among the included studies.
Including retrospective studies introduced a risk of confounding, and researchers’ awareness of treatment introduced a risk of detection bias.
Many included articles did not clearly characterize or report hypogonadal symptoms alongside biochemical outcomes.
Missing data for sizeable portions of some study populations limit conclusions about metabolic and lipid outcomes.
strengths: The authors describe this as the first systematic review with meta-analysis on this question to include both RCTs and observational cohort studies, with a large combined study population.
They used a validated quality-assessment instrument applicable to the different included study designs.
Including RCTs and observational studies may better reflect patients seen in routine clinical practice.
Results remained consistent in sensitivity analyses restricted by study design and methodological quality.
open_questions: Which CC dose is most effective, and which patient characteristics should influence dosing?
How durable is CC efficacy during long-term use and after treatment stops?
Which factors predict biochemical or clinical response to CC?
Does CC affect metabolic and lipid profiles?
What adverse effects might emerge with longer-term CC use?
future_directions: Investigate whether patient characteristics help determine CC dosing and predict treatment response.
Conduct further research to establish whether CC changes metabolic and lipid outcomes.
Assess safety with follow-up above 5 years.
Develop and implement a new or updated instrument for evaluating hypogonadal symptoms.

main_findings.description: Across the included studies, serum total testosterone was higher during clomiphene citrate treatment than before treatment.
main_findings.context: Total testosterone data were available for 98%, n = 1256 patients; I2 = 98%. Baseline study means ranged from 179.0 ng/dL (72.0) to 310.3 ng/dL (96.0), and means during treatment ranged from 467.0 ng/dL (190.0) to 687.9 ng/dL (276.7). The standardized measure accommodated studies using different units.

main_findings.description: Serum free testosterone was higher during clomiphene citrate treatment than before treatment.
main_findings.context: Reported in five studies (17%, n = 222); I2 = 95%. The studies used different measurement units.

main_findings.description: Serum luteinizing hormone was higher during clomiphene citrate treatment than before treatment.
main_findings.context: Reported in eight studies (24%, n = 301); I2 = 77%.

main_findings.description: Serum follicle stimulating hormone was higher during clomiphene citrate treatment than before treatment.
main_findings.context: Reported in six studies (14%, n = 180); I2 = 72%.

main_findings.description: Serum estradiol was higher during clomiphene citrate treatment than before treatment.
main_findings.context: The article describes eight studies (47%, n = 595); I2 = 82%.

main_findings.description: ADAM scores decreased during clomiphene citrate treatment, indicating improved reported symptoms.
main_findings.context: Four studies (14%, n = 176); I2 = 80%. The article prints the confidence-interval notation as shown.

main_findings.description: The reported overall total-testosterone response rate varied across studies.
main_findings.context: Three studies defined response as a total-testosterone rise of at least 200 ng/dL over baseline and a level above 400– 450 ng/dL.

main_findings.description: Four studies found greater total testosterone during clomiphene citrate treatment than with anastrozole, placebo, or no therapy.

One study found higher luteinizing hormone and follicle stimulating hormone with clomiphene citrate than with placebo, whereas another found no difference in either hormone between clomiphene citrate and anastrozole.
main_findings.context: These are between-treatment findings, distinct from the pooled before-and-during-treatment changes.

main_findings.description: The studies reported differences in estradiol during clomiphene citrate treatment relative to placebo and anastrozole.
main_findings.context: The article does not provide a pooled effect estimate for these between-treatment comparisons.

main_findings.description: In the sensitivity analyses restricted by study design or methodological quality, the results for total testosterone, free testosterone, estradiol, luteinizing hormone, and follicle stimulating hormone continued to favor measurements during treatment and remained statistically significant.
main_findings.context: The design-restricted analysis included four RCTs; the quality-restricted analysis included three studies. An ADAM sensitivity analysis could not be repeated because only one study remained.

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: Four studies (36%, n = 590) reported clomiphene citrate side effects in 4% to 11% of their populations; seven studies (20%, n = 332) reported none. The abstract describes reported side effects as occurring in less than 10% of study populations, while the results section gives an upper value of 11%.
notable_adverse_events: Mood changes were among the side effects reported with clomiphene citrate; an event-specific rate was not given.
Blurred vision was among the side effects reported with clomiphene citrate; an event-specific rate was not given.
Breast/nipple tenderness was among the side effects reported with clomiphene citrate; an event-specific rate was not given.
Fatigue was among the side effects reported with clomiphene citrate; an event-specific rate was not given.
Weight gain and headache were identified among the more frequently reported side effects of clomiphene citrate; event-specific rates were not given.
One clomiphene citrate-treated patient in a study of 24%, n = 400 had elevated Ht, which the authors described as having no clinical significance.
An included study described a paradoxical deterioration in testicular function in two patients receiving clomiphene citrate; its underlying cause was unclear.

A study of 2%, n = 34 found no difference between clomiphene citrate and placebo in self-reported somnolence, weight gain, acne, asthenia, irritability, changes in bowel habits, anxiety, increased appetite, urethral candidiasis, headache, perceived testicular reduction, snoring, or cramps.
No serious adverse events were reported.

subgroup_analyses: Three studies compared hormonal outcomes by age. One study (1%, n = 17) found a difference in total testosterone during treatment between men with median ages of 53 years and 66 years. Another (8%, n = 125) found a larger increase during clomiphene citrate treatment at ages 30-50 year than above 50 years. A third (2%, n = 36) did not find higher total testosterone in either of its two age groups.
In Guay et al. (2003), increasing age was associated with a decreasing response in attempted sexual intercourse during clomiphene citrate treatment (11%, n = 178; p = 0.028).
An included study found greater subjective symptom improvement among clomiphene citrate-treated patients aged <55 years of age (5%, n = 86).

In a double-blind, placebo-controlled study (1%, n = 17), the younger group (median 53, range 42-61) responded better to clomiphene citrate for sexual satisfaction, tip rigidity, nocturnal tumescence, and intercourse attempts; patients nevertheless could not distinguish clomiphene citrate from placebo by symptom improvement.

In Shabsigh (2005), total testosterone during treatment was 579.7 (152.7) ng/dL in G1: ≤ 40 year and 652.4 (207.6) ng/dL in G2: > 40 year, compared with respective pretreatment values of 251.4 (38.9) and 242.2 (41.8) ng/dL.

In Da Ros (2012), total testosterone before and during treatment was 329.18 (87.76) and 794.59 (231.05) ng/dL for G1: ≤ 50 year; 296.41 (85.53) and 648.35 (238.13) ng/dL for G2: 50–70 year; and 335.30 (124.08) and 624.03 (224.53) ng/dL for G3: > 70 year. The reported comparisons with G1 were p = 0.04 for G2 and p = 0.006 for G3.
secondary_results: The review included 19 studies—four RCTs and 15 observational cohort studies—and 1642 patients treated with clomiphene citrate. Seventeen studies with 1279 treated patients entered the meta-analysis. Among the observational studies, 11 were retrospective and four prospective.
EPHPP assessments rated 3 included studies strong, 5 moderate, and 11 weak. Treatment and follow-up across studies varied between one and a half and 52 months.
Twelve studies assessed hypogonadal symptoms using ADAM, qADAM, IIEF-5, EHS, or monthly intercourse events (49%, n = 798).

One study (5%, n = 86) reported improvement in 5 out of 10 ADAM items during clomiphene citrate treatment. Its reported improvements included libido, energy, enjoyment of life, mood, and sports performance; 10% of patients did not report symptomatic improvement.

A placebo group also improved on ADAM in one study (2%, n = 34). A separate placebo-controlled study (n = 17) found that participants could not distinguish symptom improvement during clomiphene citrate treatment from improvement during placebo. Another RCT reported comparable overall improvement in its clomiphene citrate and placebo groups, although erection strength improved in the clomiphene citrate group and libido improved in both groups.
One study found no qADAM difference between clomiphene citrate and anastrozole (1%, n = 13). In Habous (2018), qADAM scores were only marginally higher with CC + hCG than with hCG or CC alone.

Four studies assessed BMI before and during treatment (11%, n = 184). Only one reported a decrease after 3 years of clomiphene citrate treatment; the other reported comparisons did not establish a difference.

Three studies assessed total cholesterol before and during treatment (14%, n = 224). One (8%, n = 125) found a decrease during clomiphene citrate treatment, whereas the other studies did not find that effect.

In Da Ros (2012), mean total cholesterol in the CC group changed from 197.50 (39.03) to 187.35 (37.48) mg/dL (p = 0.001). In Soares (2018), the CC group's corresponding values were 199.9 (35.6) and 189.8 (28.9) mg/dL (n = 35; n.s.). In Taylor (2010), they were 171 (n.a.) and 203 (n.a.) mg/dL (p = 0.4) for CC, and 199 (n.a.) and 182 (n.a.) mg/dL (p = 0.19) for T gel.
Across the reported safety measurements, Hb, Ht, total PSA, IPSS, and BP did not differ before versus during clomiphene citrate treatment.

One study (2.8%, n = 46) found improved femoral-neck and lumbar-spine bone density over 1, 2, and 3 years of clomiphene citrate treatment. The proportion with normal bone density was 28% before treatment and 50%, 48%, and 55% at 1 year, 2 years, and 3 years, respectively; the study reported fewer patients with osteoporosis over time.
In the included longer-term studies (n = 29-120), serum hormonal responses persisted during 24 till 52 months of clomiphene citrate use.

After a trial withdrawal of clomiphene citrate in Patel et al. (2015) (n = 27), 78% had total testosterone <300 ng/dL after 3 months, and all patients had total testosterone <300 ng/dL after 6 months. The article contrasts this finding with differing results from other studies after treatment cessation.
Krzastek et al. (2019) (n = 400) reported subjective improvement in hypogonadal symptoms in >75% of patients with FU > 3 years.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Background: Male hypogonadism combines clinical manifestations with biochemical androgen insufficiency and becomes more common with age. Exogenous testosterone is the preferred initial treatment, but its suppression of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis reduces intratesticular testosterone production and spermatogenesis. Clomiphene citrate is used off-label to treat hypogonadism while preserving these functions. This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed its effectiveness and safety. Methods: EMBASE, PubMed and Cochrane were searched in May 2021 for interventional and observational effectiveness studies in men with hypogonadism. Study quality was assessed with the Effective Public Health Practice Project Quality Assessment Tool. The primary outcome was serum hormone concentration; secondary outcomes covered symptoms, metabolic and lipid measures, adverse effects and safety. Results: The review included 19 studies—four randomized controlled trials and 15 observational studies—with 1642 patients. The meta-analysis included 17 studies and 1279 patients. Treatment and follow-up ranged from one and a half to 52 months. Total testosterone increased by 2.60 (95% CI 1.82–3.38) during clomiphene citrate treatment. Free testosterone, luteinizing hormone, follicle stimulating hormone, sex hormone-binding globulin and estradiol also increased. Studies used different symptom measures; the most common, the Androgen Deficiency in Aging Males questionnaire, showed improvement during treatment. The abstract reports adverse effects in less than 10% of study populations and no serious adverse events. Conclusion: The authors conclude that clomiphene citrate improves biochemical and clinical manifestations of male hypogonadism, with few reported adverse effects and a favorable safety profile.

document_sections.heading: 1 BACKGROUND
document_sections.content: Hypogonadism is common in men. The European Association of Urology characterizes it as clinical and biochemical testosterone insufficiency that affects organ function and quality of life. Manifestations include erectile dysfunction, reduced sexual activity and desire, mood changes, and diminished muscle strength. Symptomatic hypogonadism at ages 40–79 years has a prevalence between 2.1% and 5.7%; prevalence rises with age and with obesity, cardiovascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diabetes mellitus (DM) type 2, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), chronic kidney disease, malignancy or metabolic syndrome. Causes can be located at different levels of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis. Primary hypogonadism, described as the most frequent type, arises from testicular failure and features low serum testosterone with high gonadotropins; Klinefelter syndrome and testicular tumors are common causes. Secondary hypogonadism reflects inadequate gonadotropin stimulation of the testes and usually involves reduced or inappropriately normal gonadotropins; examples of causes are hyperprolactinemia, Kallmann’s syndrome and obesity. Adult-onset or late-onset hypogonadism denotes symptomatic testosterone deficiency in middle-aged or older men whose HPG-axis function is normal. Testosterone therapy (TTh) is the first-choice treatment. It aims to raise serum testosterone and restore androgen-dependent functions, including muscle mass and strength, sexual function, bone density and general well-being. Its adverse effects include subfertility, particularly important for men who want children now or later: negative feedback reduces endogenous testosterone. Other reported effects include increased prostate volume, prostate specific antigen (PSA), hematocrit (Ht) and serum estrogen, as well as altered serum lipids. Fertility preservation and cost can discourage TTh prescribing. Other medications used include human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), aromatase inhibitors, and selective estrogen/androgen receptor modulators (SERMS and SARMS). Clomiphene citrate (CC), a SERM, occupies estrogen receptors in the hypothalamus and pituitary. The resulting gonadotropin release increases testicular stimulation and testosterone production. CC has been used for ovulation induction in women from 1960. Its use in men is off-label; the US Food And Drug Administration (FDA) had not approved it because its effectiveness was unclear. Studies and reviews have addressed CC for subfertility, but few specifically assessed men with hypogonadism. The authors therefore undertook a systematic review and meta-analysis to determine whether CC is effective and safe for this population.

document_sections.heading: 2 METHODS
document_sections.content: The systematic review and meta-analysis followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA), a reporting framework for reviews of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies. Its PROSPERO registration was CRD42021246588.

document_sections.heading: 2.1 Search strategy
document_sections.content: EMBASE, PubMed and Cochrane were searched systematically in May 2021. Search terms combined hypogonadism as the target population with CC as the intervention. Outcome terms were deliberately omitted so that the search could capture any reported outcome. Reference lists of included articles and relevant reviews were searched manually for additional studies. Database-specific search strings were placed in Appendix 1.

document_sections.heading: 2.2 Eligibility criteria and study selection
document_sections.content: Eligible English- or Dutch-language interventional and observational studies evaluated CC effectiveness in men with hypogonadism aged ≥ 18 years. They had to assess hormones and preferably symptoms during CC treatment. Studies of enclomiphene, zuclomiphene or CC combined with another medicine were excluded. Populations selected for specific chronic conditions—including HIV, cancer, osteoporosis, severe kidney/liver disease, depression, hemochromatosis, acromegaly, polycythemia, Alzheimer, eating disorder, sickle cell disease and retardation—or genetic disorders such as Klinefelter, Prader–Willi, Kallman and Bardet–Biedl were excluded. Further exclusions were case series n < 5, letters to the editor, pilot studies, reviews, comments and animal studies. Publication year, treatment dose and intervention duration were unrestricted. H.v.B. and M.H. selected studies independently under predefined criteria and settled disagreements through discussion. Selection proceeded through title screening and duplicate removal, abstract screening, and full-text eligibility assessment.

document_sections.heading: 2.3 Data extraction and methodological quality assessment
document_sections.content: H.v.B. and M.H. separately extracted authorship, publication year, design and study type, single- or multi-center status, patient numbers, subgroups, treatment dose, follow-up, subfertility, mean age and comorbidities. Hormone measurements before and during treatment were the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes were hypogonadal symptoms, metabolic and lipid profiles, adverse effects and safety measures. The tables marked unavailable primary or secondary values accordingly. Both reviewers independently assessed every included study using the Effective Public Health Practice Project Quality Assessment Tool (EPHPP). The authors describe this validated tool as suitable for effectiveness reviews and for different designs, including RCTs, before-and-after studies and observational studies. Its reported inter-assessor coefficient was 0.77 (95% CI, 0.51-0.90), considered excellent agreement.

document_sections.heading: 2.4 Statistical analysis
document_sections.content: Data were presented as counts, percentages or means with standard deviations (SD). Outcomes reported by three or more studies were pooled using Review Manager (RevMan) 5.4 when means and SD were available. Standard errors were converted to SD, and medians with interquartile ranges were converted to means with SD. Inverse-variance weighting yielded pooled before-versus-during-treatment mean differences or standardized mean differences with confidence intervals (CI). Standardized mean differences accommodated outcomes expressed in different units, such as nmol/L and ng/dL for TT. Forest plots, the χ2 test and the I2 statistic were used to assess heterogeneity. The stated interpretation of I2 was 0%-40% for heterogeneity that might not be important, 30%-60% for potentially moderate, 50%90% for potentially substantial, and 75%-100% for potentially considerable heterogeneity. Post-primary sensitivity analyses restricted studies by design to RCTs or by methodological quality to strongly rated studies.

document_sections.heading: 3.1 Study selection
document_sections.content: The search found 569 studies. Removing duplicates and excluding records by title left 415; abstract screening or application of prespecified exclusion criteria removed 383, leaving 32 for full-text assessment. A further 13 were excluded: full text was unavailable for 9, methods accounted for three, and outcome reporting for one. One methods-based exclusion lacked a treatment-dose description and appeared to overlap with the population in Ramasamy et al. (2014). Another evaluated a 10-day clomiphene challenge, and the third enrolled men on the basis of subfertility. The outcome-based exclusion did not clearly describe serum testosterone and symptoms. The systematic review ultimately included 19 studies; 17 entered the meta-analysis. The other two lacked both SD and interquartile-range data. FIGURE 1 depicts the study-selection process.

document_sections.heading: 3.2 Study characteristics
document_sections.content: The 19 included studies comprised four RCTs and 15 observational cohorts; 11 cohorts were retrospective and four prospective. The authors confirmed limited overlap between the populations in Patel et al. (2015) and Keihani et al. (2020), and among Katz et al. (2012), Moskovic et al. (2012) and Mazolla et al. (2014). Despite overlap, treatment durations and outcomes differed. Across the review, 1642 patients received CC. The 17 studies reporting means with SD contributed 1279 CC-treated patients to the meta-analysis. Two of these studies reported age-based subgroups; the authors selected each larger subgroup for pooling. Mean CC treatment duration and follow-up ranged between one and a half and 52 months. Mean age ranged between 29 and 62 years; one study confined enrollment to young patients with obesity aged between 19 and 21 years. CC doses ranged between 25 and 50 mg per day or 25, 50, or 100 mg every other day. TABLE 1 presents study and patient characteristics, treatment regimens, follow-up and EPHPP ratings; Appendix 2 provides additional characteristics.

document_sections.heading: 3.3 Methodological quality assessment
document_sections.content: Under EPHPP, 3 of the 19 studies received a strong rating, 5 a moderate rating and 11 a weak rating. TABLE 1 identifies study-level ratings, and Appendix 3 contains further assessment details.

document_sections.heading: 3.4 Hormonal evaluation
document_sections.content: TABLES 2 and 3 present hormone concentrations before and during treatment; FIGURES 2, 3 and 4 depict pooled comparisons for testosterone, gonadotropins and estradiol. Across studies, mean (SD) total testosterone (TT) at baseline ranged between 179.0 ng/dL (72.0) and 310.3 ng/dL (96.0), versus between 467.0 ng/dL (190.0) and 687.9 ng/dL (276.7) during treatment. Before-and-during TT data were available from 17 of the 17 meta-analyzed studies (98%, n = 1256 patients); one study’s median (IQR) was converted to a mean (SD). Because TT units differed between nmol/L and ng/dL, the pooled effect was standardized: TT was higher during CC treatment, with a standardized mean difference of 2.60 (95% CI, 1.82, 3.38; p < 0.00001; I2 = 98%). Four studies found TT improvement with CC compared with anastrozole, placebo or no therapy. Three studies reported overall response rates between 62% and 81%, defining response as a TT increase of at least 200 ng/dL over baseline and a level above 400– 450 ng/dL. Five studies reported mean (SD) free testosterone (FT) before and during treatment (17%, n = 222). Because FT was measured in pmol/L or ng/dL, its pooled effect was standardized: FT was higher during treatment, with a standardized mean difference of 1.78 (95% CI, 0.65, 2.91; p = 0.002; I2 = 95%). Eight studies reported mean (SD) luteinizing hormone (LH) before and during treatment (24%, n = 301); the treatment-period increase had a mean difference of 4.67 IU/L (95% CI, 3.67, 5.68; p < 0.00001; I2 = 77%). Six studies supplied corresponding follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) data (14%, n = 180), with a mean difference of 4.25 IU/L (95% CI, 2.70, 5.81; p < 0.00001; I2 = 72%) favoring treatment. One study found higher LH and FSH with CC than placebo during treatment; another found no CC–anastrozole difference for those hormones. Eight studies reported mean (SD) serum estradiol before and during treatment (47%, n = 595). Estradiol was higher during treatment, with a mean difference of 17.69 pg/ml (95% CI, 12.46, 22.92; p < 0.00001; I2 = 82%); treatment-period differences were also identified against placebo and anastrozole. Three studies compared hormone outcomes by age. One (1%, n = 17) found a treatment-period TT difference between younger men (median 53 years) and older men (median 66 years). Another (8%, n = 125) found a larger TT increase in patients aged 30-50 year than in those above 50 years. The third (2%, n = 36) found no higher TT in either age group.

document_sections.heading: 3.5 Symptoms of hypogonadism
document_sections.content: Twelve studies assessed symptoms (49%, n = 798) using the Androgen Deficiency in Aging Males (ADAM), quantitative ADAM score (qADAM), International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF-5), Erection Hardness Scale (EHS) or monthly intercourse-event counts. TABLE 4 presents symptom assessments before and during CC; FIGURE 5 depicts the pooled ADAM comparison. Four studies (14%, n = 176) showed ADAM improvement during CC. Because lower scores indicate improvement, the pooled mean difference was −3.13 (95%, 4.16, 2.10; p < 0.00001; I2 = 80%). One study (5%, n = 86) found improvement in 5 out of 10 ADAM items. ADAM scores also improved in a placebo group in another study (2%, n = 34). One study found no CC–anastrozole difference on qADAM (1%, n = 13). In a study of intercourse attempts, increasing age was associated with reduced response to CC (p = 0.028; 11%, n = 178). Another study (5%, n = 86) found greater subjective symptom improvement in patients aged <55 years. A further study (1%, n = 17) found that the younger group (median 53, range 42-61) responded better on sexual satisfaction, tip rigidity, nocturnal tumescence and intercourse attempts; nevertheless, participants in that double-blind, placebo-controlled trial could not distinguish CC from placebo on the basis of symptoms.

document_sections.heading: 3.6 Lipid and metabolic profile
document_sections.content: Four studies reported BMI before and during treatment (11%, n = 184). Only one found a BMI decrease after 3 years of CC; overall, no before-versus-during-treatment BMI difference was found. Three studies reported total cholesterol at both times (14%, n = 224). Only one (8%, n = 125) found a reduction during CC treatment. TABLE 5 presents metabolic and lipid measurements by study and treatment group.

document_sections.heading: 3.7 Safety aspects and side effects
document_sections.content: TABLE 6 presents before-and-during-treatment hemoglobin (Hb), Ht, PSA, International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), blood pressure (BP) and bone-density findings from four studies. No differences were found for Hb, Ht, total PSA, IPSS or BP. One study (24%, n = 400) reported one CC-treated patient with elevated Ht, without clinical significance. A bone-density study (2.8%, n = 46) found improvement at the femoral neck and lumbar spine over 1, 2, and 3 years: bone density rose and the proportion of patients with osteoporosis fell over time. Seven studies (20%, n = 332) reported no CC adverse effects. Four (36%, n = 590) reported adverse effects in between 4% and 11% of their populations, including mood changes, blurred vision, breast/nipple tenderness and fatigue. One study (2%, n = 34) found no CC–placebo difference in self-reported somnolence, weight gain, acne, asthenia, irritability, altered bowel habits, anxiety, increased appetite, urethral candidiasis, headache, perceived testicular reduction, snoring or cramps.

document_sections.heading: 3.8 Sensitivity analyses
document_sections.content: The study-design sensitivity analysis included four RCTs; the methodological-quality analysis included three studies. ADAM could not be reanalyzed because only one study remained. The other five analyses—TT, FT, estradiol, LH and FSH—were repeated. Every repeated result continued to favor measurements during treatment and remained statistically significant.

document_sections.heading: 4 DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: The authors interpret their review as showing higher TT and improved ADAM symptoms during CC treatment in men with hypogonadism; the reported overall TT response rate was between 62% and 81%. They describe it as, to their knowledge, the first meta-analysis on this question to combine RCTs with observational cohorts. FT, LH, FSH and estradiol also rose. The authors regard the testosterone and gonadotropin changes as evidence that CC stimulates the HPG-axis and endogenous testosterone secretion. They state that treatment-period TT reached the reference value (15.6-20.8 nmol//L) cited from American Urology Association guidelines as sufficient for treating hypogonadism. In comparisons cited by the authors, Taylor and Levine (2010) (n = 103) found no serum-TT difference between CC and testosterone gel. Ramasamy et al. (2014) (n = 124) likewise found comparable CC and testosterone-gel effects, but a larger TT increase with testosterone injections than with either; that study found no ADAM difference between TTh and CC. The authors describe CC as less expensive, noninvasive and fertility-sparing relative to TTh. They note that testosterone injections produce a high exogenous-TT peak with a potentially greater adverse-effect risk. The most effective CC dose and the patient characteristics influencing it remain undetermined. Included doses varied between 25 and 50 mg/day and 25, 50, or 100 mg every other day. Keihani et al. (2020) used bioavailable testosterone, BMI, patient preferences and symptom severity to choose doses, but the relevance of these factors lacks supporting evidence. Four included studies adjusted CC doses according to TT measured after treatment had begun. The authors’ proposed current strategy is to begin with the lowest dose, 25 mg every other day, and titrate according to achieved serum TT or symptom improvement. Follow-up across included studies ranged from 1.5 to 52 months. Most studies described an effective biochemical response within the first month. A cited clomiphene challenge test found TT above 400 ng/dL after 7 days and above 500 ng/dL after 10 days. Whether benefit persists after stopping CC and how well long-term treatment works remain important questions. Three included studies (n = 29-120) reported sustained serum-hormone responses after 24 till 52 months of use; the authors describe these as, to their knowledge, the longest and largest studies of long-term CC effectiveness for male hypogonadism. Evidence about TT after stopping CC conflicts. Guay et al. (2003) proposed that TT might remain stable after withdrawal, but did not test the proposition. In contrast, Patel et al. (2015) (n = 27) interrupted treatment and found TT <300 ng/dL in 78% after 3 months and in all patients after 6 months. In a separate study of five patients assessed 5-7 months after withdrawal, TT decreased but remained above 400 ng/dL in three, whereas two returned to pretreatment concentrations. Another study found normal TT 6 months after cessation in 12 out of 16 patients and pretreatment concentrations in four. The authors characterize post-withdrawal findings as conflicting, while noting that most studies reported a TT decrease. Predictors of CC response also remain uncertain. Mazzola et al. (2014) (n = 76) identified low LH and larger testicular volume as predictors of better response. Guay et al. (2003) (n = 178) identified age and diabetes and found younger patients 2.3 as likely to respond as patients aged 56 years and older; its success measure was successful intercourse attempts, not a biochemical outcome. A different study reported TT-response rates of 100% and 32% in younger and older groups, respectively. A 10-day challenge test reported a TT value 60 ng/dL higher among participants below 50 years. Conversely, another included study (n = 36) found better TT response in older men using a lower age threshold of 40 years. Three other included studies found no association of testosterone change with gonadotropins, age, BMI, estradiol or testicular axis. Clinical response matters alongside biochemical response when characterizing hypogonadism, yet most included articles did not clearly describe and report symptoms as a major outcome. Krzastek et al. (2019) (n = 400) reported subjective symptom improvement in >75% with FU > 3 years. ADAM is a commonly used, validated screening questionnaire with relatively high sensitivity but low specificity; pooled ADAM scores improved. One included study (n = 86) found improvement in decreased libido, lack of energy, reduced enjoyment of life, sad or irritable mood, and reduced sports performance, although 10% did not experience symptom improvement. The authors urge caution in interpreting symptom findings: a placebo-controlled RCT (n = 17) from 1995 found that patients could not tell CC periods from placebo periods by symptom improvement, and another placebo-controlled RCT found comparable overall improvement in both groups. The latter study found better erection strength with CC and improved libido in both groups when it examined individual items. The authors suggest that differences in symptom severity might explain some findings and conclude that hypogonadal symptoms have multiple causes that one questionnaire cannot readily capture. They advocate developing and implementing a new or updated questionnaire. Evidence for lipid and metabolic effects remains inconclusive. BMI differed in only one out of four studies; one included study (n = 125) found lower total cholesterol during treatment, while two others did not. Missing data for substantial portions of several study populations further support the authors’ call for research into metabolic and lipid effects. Most included studies reported no adverse effects. Among reported effects, the authors identify mood changes, blurred vision, breast/nipple tenderness, weight gain and headache as most frequent; they describe their incidence and type as comparable to CC use in women. Elevated hematocrit could potentially lead to thrombo-embolic events, but only one included patient had elevated hematocrit. An earlier cited study of 200 CC-treated patients found less polycythemia with CC than TTh and no hematocrit elevation requiring phlebotomy. Cited case reports in women linked thrombosis during CC treatment to CC-associated ovarian hyperstimulation. Two patients in one included study had a paradoxical reversal of CC’s effect on testicular function; its underlying cause is unclear, and case series had previously described it. The authors call for CC follow-up above 5 years to determine long-term adverse effects. Limitations include the possibility that the search missed studies despite its extensive database and reference-list searches; substantial heterogeneity in most analyses given the limited evidence base; variation in study design, CC dose and hormone assays; and poorly specified or non-strict eligibility criteria in some included studies. Methodological quality varied. Retrospective designs introduce potential confounding, and investigators’ knowledge of treatment introduces potential detection bias. The authors also identify strengths: a large study population, use of a validated quality-assessment instrument applicable across designs, inclusion of RCTs and observational studies that may better represent routine clinical populations, and consistency of findings in sensitivity analyses restricted by design and quality.

document_sections.heading: 5 CONCLUSION
document_sections.content: The authors conclude that CC improves both symptoms and biochemical testosterone insufficiency in men with hypogonadism, with few reported adverse effects and favorable safety findings. They consider continued treatment probably necessary to maintain biochemical and clinical effects. In their opinion, CC is a potentially effective and safe option that should be considered for symptomatic hypogonadism, particularly when a man wishes to have children now or in the future.

tables.summary: The table reports baseline and on-treatment hormone values for CC and, where available, comparison groups and age subgroups. Its interleaved subgroup entries make some study labels inconsistent with the accompanying discussion; those entries should not be treated as unambiguous study-level comparisons. In the review's pooled analysis, on-treatment TT exceeded baseline by a standardized mean difference of 2.60 (95% CI, 1.82, 3.38; p < 0.00001; I2 = 98%).

tables.summary: Symptom instruments and available measurements differ substantially across studies. ADAM scores declined during CC treatment in several cohorts, but a placebo group also improved, and the review cautions against treating questionnaire changes as a uniform clinical response. The Marconi (2016) ED subgroup range is internally inconsistent with its accompanying median.

tables.summary: The studies report limited metabolic follow-up. The review identifies a BMI reduction in only one study and a total-cholesterol reduction in Da Ros (2012), without a consistent cholesterol effect in the other studies. Some row labels and participant counts in this table differ from the corresponding study-characteristics table.

tables.summary: Across the reported safety measurements, the review describes no difference in Hb, Ht, PSA, IPSS or BP before versus during CC treatment. Krzastek (2019) recorded one elevated-Ht patient without clinical significance, while Moskovic (2012) reported an increasing proportion with normal bone density. The table lists T gel = 39 for Taylor (2010), whereas the study-characteristics table lists T gel = 38.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that clomiphene citrate may improve testosterone deficiency and hypogonadal symptoms while having relatively few reported adverse effects. They consider it a potentially effective and safe option for symptomatic men, particularly those who wish to have children now or later, and suggest that continued treatment is probably needed to maintain its effects.
narrative_summary:
This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated clomiphene citrate for men with hypogonadism. It included 19 studies—four RCTs and 15 observational studies—with 1642 CC-treated patients; 17 studies comprising 1279 patients contributed to the meta-analysis. Compared with pretreatment values, total testosterone increased by a standardized mean difference of 2.60 (95% CI, 1.82, 3.38; p < 0.00001; I2 = 98%). Free testosterone, LH, FSH and estradiol also rose during treatment. The reported total-testosterone response rate ranged from 62% to 81%.

ADAM scores improved during CC treatment, although placebo groups also showed symptom improvement in some trials. The authors therefore urge caution when interpreting symptomatic benefit. Findings for BMI and cholesterol were inconsistent, and they state that evidence for metabolic and lipid effects remains insufficient. Most studies reported no adverse effects; reported events included mood changes, blurred vision, breast/nipple tenderness, weight gain and headache. One study identified an elevated hematocrit in one patient without clinical significance.

The evidence is limited by substantial heterogeneity, varying doses and measurements, differences in methodological quality, and possible confounding in retrospective studies. The authors view CC as a treatment to consider for symptomatic men, especially those with a current or future wish for children. They also judge continued therapy probably necessary to preserve biochemical and clinical effects.
